title: 1 Chronicles 23:1–6
context: Chronicles reports in a single sentence that David, old and full of days, made Solomon his son king over Israel; the fuller account of Solomon’s accession, including Adonijah’s bid for the throne, is told in 1 Kings 1, and Chronicles later says Solomon was made king a second time (1 Chronicles 29:22). David then gathers the princes, priests, and Levites and numbers the Levites from thirty years old and upward, thirty-eight thousand men, assigning them to oversee the work of the LORD’s house, to serve as officers and judges, as doorkeepers, and as musicians. The age of thirty here matches Numbers 4:3, while 23:24 and 23:27 speak of twenty years old and upward and Numbers 8:24 of twenty-five; the text names these figures without explaining how they relate. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read the passage as shared ground about worship ordered with care, many kinds of service, and David preparing for the temple his son would build.

verses.text: Now David was old and full of days; and he made Solomon his son king over Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Chronicles summarizes Solomon’s accession in one sentence, with the fuller story told in 1 Kings 1. The focus here falls on David preparing the next generation for worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the transfer of the throne as part of God’s purpose in choosing Solomon (compare 1 Chronicles 28:5). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a brief frame for the organization of worship that follows.

verses.text: He gathered together all the princes of Israel, with the priests and the Levites.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David gathering princes, priests, and Levites together. Political and religious leaders work side by side in preparing for the temple.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the assembly as showing that worship concerns the whole covenant community. Both traditions commonly read the verse as an act of careful, shared planning.

verses.text: The Levites were counted from thirty years old and upward; and their number by their polls, man by man, was thirty-eight thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the Levites are counted from thirty years old and upward, numbering thirty-eight thousand. The age matches Numbers 4:3, while later verses mention twenty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the census as preparation for orderly service rather than a display of strength. Readers in both traditions commonly leave the differences in age figures unresolved, as the text does.

verses.text: David said, “Of these, twenty-four thousand were to oversee the work of the LORD’s house, six thousand were officers and judges,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see twenty-four thousand assigned to oversee the work of the LORD’s house and six thousand as officers and judges. Service in worship and justice are both valued.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the allocation as showing that administration and justice belong within God’s ordering of his people. Both traditions commonly read the verse as honoring diverse callings.

verses.text: four thousand were doorkeepers, and four thousand praised the LORD with the instruments which I made for giving praise.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see four thousand doorkeepers and four thousand musicians praising the LORD with instruments David made. Guarding and praising are both acts of worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see music in worship as part of David’s careful ordering (compare Psalm 84:10 for the honor of doorkeeping). Readers in both traditions commonly see dignity in every assigned role.

verses.text: David divided them into divisions according to the sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David dividing the Levites according to Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Family lines provide structure for service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see continuity with the order given in the wilderness (compare Numbers 3:17). Both traditions commonly read the verse as grounding new arrangements in God’s earlier provision.
